```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
library(NECorr)
```

NECorr ranks the genes of a molecular network for their importance in one
condition, using expression data measured across several conditions.

# Example data

The package ships a small simulated data set: a regulatory network of 12
transcription factors, and expression of 120 genes in four conditions.
`Gene001` and its targets are co-expressed and induced in flower.

```{r}
data(necorr_example)
head(necorr_example$networkFile, 3)
necorr_example$expression[1:3, 1:5]
head(necorr_example$meta_data, 3)
head(necorr_example$description.file, 3)
```

The same data are available as text files, and `NECorr()` accepts file paths:

```{r}
list.files(system.file("extdata", package = "NECorr"), pattern = "^example_")
```

# Running NECorr

```{r}
res <- NECorr(
  networkFile      = necorr_example$networkFile,
  expression       = necorr_example$expression,
  description.file = necorr_example$description.file,
  meta_data        = necorr_example$meta_data,
  condition        = "flower",
  method           = "GCC",
  permutation      = 200,
  directed         = TRUE,
  n_null           = 50,
  visualize        = FALSE,
  save_results     = FALSE,
  verbose          = FALSE
)
```

`method` can be one or several of `"GCC"` (Gini), `"PCC"` (Pearson), `"SCC"`
(Spearman) and `"KCC"` (Kendall). `permutation` is the number of permutations
for the GCC p-value. `n_null` adds an empirical p-value per gene.

# Results

Ranked genes. `Gene001` and its targets are expected at the top.

```{r}
head(res$necorrHub_nodes, 8)
```

The criteria behind the score, each as a rank between 0 and 1, and their weights:

```{r}
round(head(res$hub.m.param[res$necorrHub_nodes$Gene, ], 5), 2)
round(res$criterion_weights, 3)
```

Candidate regulators, ordered by their own score. The enrichment of top-scoring genes among their targets is shown alongside.

```{r}
head(res$necorrReg[, c("Gene", "role", "n_partners", "n_hub_partners", "fold_enrichment", "FDR")], 5)
```

Top-ranked edges. `percentile` is a rank among all edges, not a p-value.

```{r}
head(res$necorrEdges, 5)
```

What was run:

```{r}
str(res$settings[c("weights", "aggregation", "direction", "scaling", "degree_type", "directed")])
```

# Criteria, weights and aggregation

By default the score is the rank product of two criteria. `DE` is the
differential expression of the condition against the mean of the other
conditions, counted only when the gene is up-regulated (`direction = "up"`).
`Degree` is the number of targets of the gene in a directed network, and the
number of partners in an undirected one (`degree_type`). Each is turned into a
rank divided by the number of genes and the score is their geometric mean, so
there is no weight to choose and up-regulated regulators with many targets
come first. This default was selected on human cancer cell lines, where
genome-wide CRISPR screens give a complete ground truth.

Four further criteria can be added. `TS` measures how consistently the gene is
higher in the condition than in every other condition. `Coexpr` counts the
network partners that are strongly co-expressed with the gene and compares the
count with random partners drawn as in a degree-preserving randomisation of the
network. `CondCoexpr` is `Coexpr` restricted to the part of the correlation
that comes from the samples of the condition. `Bridging` is betweenness
centrality beyond what degree predicts.

A ranking that uses only the wiring and the expression, with weights from the
Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP):

```{r}
c3 <- c("Coexpr", "TS", "CondCoexpr")
A <- necorr_ahp_matrix(c3, preset = "wiring")
round(A, 2)
ahp <- ahp_weights(A)
round(ahp$weights, 2)
ahp$CR   # consistency ratio, should be below 0.1
res_wiring <- NECorr(
  necorr_example$networkFile, necorr_example$expression, necorr_example$description.file,
  "flower", necorr_example$meta_data, method = "PCC", permutation = 0,
  criteria = c3, aggregation = "product", scaling = "softcap", weights = A,
  directed = TRUE, visualize = FALSE, save_results = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
round(res_wiring$criterion_weights, 2)
head(res_wiring$coexpression_stats[order(-res_wiring$coexpression_stats$Coexpr), c("Gene", "k", "n_strong", "Coexpr", "CondCoexpr")], 3)
```

To use your own judgements, edit the matrix (keeping it reciprocal) and pass it
as `weights`. Other options are `"critic"`, `"equal"`, `"entropy"`, or a named
numeric vector. The criteria are combined by a weighted product by default;
`aggregation = "sum"` gives the weighted sum.

```{r}
res_alt <- NECorr(
  necorr_example$networkFile, necorr_example$expression, necorr_example$description.file,
  "flower", necorr_example$meta_data, method = "PCC", permutation = 0,
  criteria = c("Coexpr", "TS", "CondCoexpr", "DE"), weights = "critic", aggregation = "sum",
  directed = TRUE, visualize = FALSE, save_results = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
round(res_alt$criterion_weights, 3)
head(res_alt$necorrHub_nodes$Gene, 8)
```

# Plots and saved files

```{r, fig.height = 4}
plots <- visualize_necorr_results(res, top_n = 15)
plots$top_hubs_plot
```

```{r, fig.height = 5}
plots$network_plot
```

With `save_results = TRUE` and an `output_dir`, `NECorr()` writes
`necorrHub_nodes.csv`, `necorrReg.csv`, `necorrEdges.csv`, `coexpres.csv`,
`hub.m.param.csv`, `netstat.csv` and `criterion_weights.csv`.

# Notes on use

- The network must be measured independently of the expression data. Do not
  use a co-expression network built from the same samples.
- Set `directed = FALSE` for protein-protein interaction networks. Genes in
  `necorrReg` are then reported as "associated", not as regulators.
- Correlations are imprecise with fewer than about 8 to 10 samples.
- The default follows up-regulation and the number of targets, so only genes
  that are regulators in the network can reach the top of the list. Give the
  network with the regulator in the first column and `directed = TRUE`.
- The co-expression criteria need network edges that are reflected in the
  expression data, and they did not improve the ranking on the human benchmark.
